news.2026-11-13-soudan-du-sud-amnesty-ma: South Sudan: Amnesty accuses the UN and the authorities of ignoring warnings before a massacre of more than 200 people

In a report published on November 12, Amnesty International says UN peacekeepers and South Sudan's authorities knew two weeks in advance that an attack threatened the town of Abiemnom, where more than 200 people were killed on March 1. The country votes in December [1][2][3].

At dawn on March 1, between 1,000 and 1,500 armed men from Mayom County, in Unity State, attacked Abiemnom for four hours, according to the report titled “The Abiemnom Massacre: Inaction and Impunity in South Sudan” [3].
The authorities count more than 200 dead, including 130 residents, 76 members of the security forces and seven foreigners [1][3].
According to Amnesty, the UN mission (UNMISS) only reinforced its three dozen or so peacekeepers on site after the attack [2][3].
The NGO is calling for an independent investigation into the killings and a separate review of the peacekeepers' response; South Sudan's authorities did not answer its two letters [1][3].

Key point: the report questions the ability of one of the UN's largest peace missions to protect civilians, just as South Sudan, the world's youngest country, prepares for elections in December [1][2].

Many fear the vote could shatter a fragile peace [1]. A country already hit by intercommunal violence loses even more of its people's trust when neither the state nor the UN acts despite warnings [3].

The direct effect on your daily life is small. But France and the European Union fund UN peace missions through their contributions: their effectiveness, or their failures, weigh on debates about aid and the stability of a region next to war-torn Sudan.
